input:
Scope

Membrane technology has attracted growing attention in recent years as an energy-efficient alternative to traditional separation methods, and solvent recovery is widely regarded as one of its most promising areas of application. This review examines the literature on membrane separations for solvent recovery, in which a membrane is used to pass the solvent of a liquid mixture while retaining dissolved material, allowing the solvent to be reused rather than distilled or discarded. The review covers a total of 148 papers published over the last 6 years, encompassing both polymeric and ceramic membranes, laboratory studies and pilot-scale work, and a wide range of solvent-bearing streams arising from reaction, extraction and washing operations. Gas separations are excluded, while aqueous separations are included only where the same membrane has also been studied with a solvent stream. It is important to note that performance in this field is generally assessed using two key parameters, namely the solvent flux and the rejection of dissolved material, and it is essential to consider these together, since a high flux is of little value if the membrane retains very little solute, and a very high rejection may be impractical if the flux is extremely low.

Established results

A number of findings are reported consistently throughout the literature and can be regarded as well established. Firstly, the solvent flux typically increases with the applied pressure difference and decreases as the viscosity of the mixture increases. Moreover, the same membrane can exhibit very different fluxes in different solvents, because the solvent interacts with the membrane material, causing it to swell and thereby altering its resistance to flow. Secondly, rejection is not a property of the membrane alone: a solute that is effectively retained in one solvent may pass through the same membrane in another, because swelling changes the relationship between the size of the solute and the size of the membrane pores. Thirdly, chemical stability is a crucial factor that limits the applicability of membrane materials, since membranes that perform well in mild solvents may soften, swell excessively or even dissolve in more aggressive solvents. Finally, concentration polarisation, in which retained material accumulates at the membrane surface, can significantly reduce flux during operation, and cross-flow operation is commonly employed to mitigate this effect. Cleaning is generally found to restore part of the flux lost during operation, although it is not reported to restore flux completely.

Disagreements

Despite the broad agreement described above, the literature contains an important area of disagreement, namely the behaviour of the flux during extended operation. Some studies report that the flux declines initially and then levels off, remaining essentially stable for the rest of the run, whereas other studies report a flux that continues to decline for as long as the run continues. Interestingly, the disagreement extends beyond the magnitude of the decline to its underlying cause, with different authors attributing the decline to compaction of the membrane under pressure, to fouling of the membrane surface, or to gradual ageing of the membrane material in the solvent. This distinction is significant in practice, because the appropriate remedy depends on the mechanism involved: fouling, for example, can potentially be managed by cleaning, whereas compaction is an inherent property of the membrane under load. Furthermore, because most experimental runs are considerably shorter than a typical service interval, the published data do not allow the disagreement to be resolved, as the runs end before the competing predictions would clearly diverge. Overall, the flux trajectory over extended operation remains an open question that short-duration studies cannot settle.

Gaps

A further issue is that certain measurements that would be highly valuable for plant design are simply not reported in the literature. In particular, nobody reports the performance of a membrane after repeated cleaning cycles: flux and rejection are measured for new membranes and, in some cases, after a single cleaning event, but not after the many fouling and cleaning cycles that a membrane would experience over its service life. This is a significant gap, because a membrane that survives one cleaning may nevertheless degrade progressively over many cycles, and purchasers ultimately need to know how a membrane performs across its whole working life rather than when it is new. In addition, there is no common test protocol across the literature, and different studies use different solutes, concentrations and run durations, which makes it difficult to compare membranes between studies on a like-for-like basis. Until these gaps are addressed and flux after repeated cleaning is routinely measured and reported on a shared basis, the selection of membranes for solvent recovery will inevitably continue to rest largely on clean-membrane performance and on a flux decline behaviour that the literature itself has not yet resolved.
target:
Scope

This review covers membrane separations for solvent recovery: processes in which a membrane passes the solvent of a liquid mixture and holds back dissolved material, so that the solvent can be returned to the process instead of being distilled or discarded. The reviewed set is 148 papers from the last 6 years. The papers cover polymeric and ceramic membranes, laboratory measurements and pilot operation, and solvent-bearing streams from reaction, extraction and washing steps. Gas separations fall outside the review, and aqueous separations are covered only where the same membrane is also reported on a solvent stream. Recovery is judged throughout on the two quantities every application must state together: the rate at which solvent passes the membrane, and the fraction of dissolved material the membrane holds back. A membrane that passes solvent quickly but holds back little solute has not performed the separation, and a membrane that holds back nearly everything but passes solvent slowly may need more area than the plant can house. The review therefore reads flux and rejection as a pair, and treats a report of either quantity alone as an incomplete account of the separation. Papers were included where the membrane, the solvent and the solute are all identified and where flux or rejection is measured rather than estimated. Papers that report a separation without identifying the membrane material fall outside the set, because a result obtained with an unnamed material can neither be repeated nor transferred to another plant's solvent stream.

Established results

Several results are reported consistently enough across the set to be treated as established. Solvent flux rises with the pressure difference across the membrane and falls as the mixture grows more viscous, and the same membrane gives different fluxes in different solvents: the solvent is not a passive carrier, because it swells the membrane material and sets the resistance the membrane presents. Rejection is decided jointly by the solute and the membrane in the solvent concerned: a solute well held back in one solvent can pass in another, because swelling opens the membrane structure and changes the size relation between solute and membrane pores. Chemical stability bounds the whole field of application. Membranes that perform well in mild solvents can soften, swell excessively or dissolve in aggressive ones, and a membrane is usable only in the solvent classes in which its material survives. Concentration polarisation — the build-up of held-back material at the membrane surface — limits flux in operation even where the clean membrane passes solvent freely, and cross-flow over the surface is the standard counter-measure. Cleaning restores part of the flux lost in service, and no report in the set treats a fouled membrane as recoverable in full by cleaning alone. A further established point concerns the reporting itself: flux stated without the pressure difference at which it was measured, and rejection stated without the feed composition, cannot be compared with any other report, and the stronger papers in the set state both conditions as a matter of course.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the flux decline during extended operation: how much flux a membrane loses as operating time accumulates, and whether the decline stops. Part of the set reports an early decline that levels off, after which flux holds steady for the remainder of the run; another part reports a decline that continues for as long as the run lasts. The disagreement is not only about the size of the decline. The two camps attribute the same observation to different causes: compaction of the membrane under pressure, fouling of the surface by held-back material, and ageing of the membrane material in the solvent are each offered as the mechanism, and the remedy each mechanism implies is different. A decline caused by compaction is a property of the membrane under load; a decline caused by fouling is a property of the stream and can be managed by cleaning. Because most runs are far shorter than a service interval, the reports cannot be reconciled from the published data: each camp's runs end before the other's predicted behaviour would separate from its own. The conflict quantity is therefore the flux trajectory over extended operation, and short runs do not settle it.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the state of the membrane after repeated cleaning cycles: flux and rejection measured after the membrane has been fouled and cleaned many times, over a period comparable with service. Papers report cleaning recovery after a single fouling event, and a membrane can survive one cleaning and still degrade over a service life of many cycles; whether rejection survives repeated cleaning is reported by none of the set. Plant design needs exactly that quantity, because a membrane is bought for its performance across its whole life, not for its performance when new. Also missing from the set is any common test protocol: membranes are compared across papers that use different solutes, different concentrations and different run lengths, so rankings between membranes rest on measurements that were never made on a common basis. Until flux after repeated cleaning is measured and reported on a shared basis, the choice between membranes for solvent recovery rests on clean-membrane performance and on a flux decline that the literature itself has not settled. Start-up behaviour is also largely unreported: the flux a membrane gives at its first contact with a solvent differs from its settled value as the material takes up solvent and compacts, and the time the settling takes is rarely stated, although a plant must be started on the unsettled membrane every time a new one is fitted.
